prompt: Why does an index that no query ever reads still cost something on a table that takes writes?
hint: Think about what an INSERT has to do with every copy of the columns.

choices.text: Every write has to update it too
choices.why: Right: an index is a copy kept current on every insert and on every update of its columns, read or not.

choices.text: The planner has to consider it for every query, and planning dominates the cost
choices.why: Planning does look at each index, but the lesson's measured cost was in the writes: 9396 against 4895 bytes of log per order.

choices.text: It holds a lock on the table while it sits unused
choices.why: An index holds no lock by existing; the locks belong to statements, which lesson 12 covers.

choices.text: It slows down reads of the other indexes
choices.why: Reads of one index are not affected by another one existing; the cost is on the writing side.

prompt: With the seven leftover indexes in place, how many bytes of write-ahead log did each order from `place-order.sql` write in the lesson's run?
hint: The second measurement, the column bytes_per_order.

prompt: Before the leftovers, 19,996 of 20,000 updates in `place-order.sql` were HOT; with them, none were. Which single leftover caused that?
hint: Which column does the UPDATE change?

choices.text: `orders_status_idx`
choices.why: The update leaves `status` alone; an index on a column the update does not change does not stop HOT.

choices.text: `orders_seller_placed_idx`, because it has two columns
choices.why: The number of columns does not matter; neither `seller_id` nor `placed_at` changes in the update.

choices.text: `orders_total_cents_idx`
choices.why: Right: the update sets `total_cents`, and HOT is only possible when no index contains a changed column.

choices.text: `orders_customer_idx`, because it duplicates another index
choices.why: Being a duplicate costs an extra entry per insert, but `customer_id` does not change in the update.

prompt: The transaction rate fell 13% with the leftovers while the log per order nearly doubled. Why does the lesson trust the log number more?
hint: What dominates one short transaction on that machine?

choices.text: Because pgbench rounds its rate to whole transactions
choices.why: pgbench prints the rate to six decimals; rounding is not the problem.

choices.text: The rate moves by several per cent between identical runs, and the log is bytes actually written
choices.why: Right: the commit's wait for the disk dominates the rate, while the log volume is a count of what the server wrote.

choices.text: The log includes reads as well as writes, so it sees more
choices.why: The write-ahead log records changes only; reads write nothing to it.

choices.text: Only the log is reset by CHECKPOINT
choices.why: A checkpoint does not reset the log position, which only grows; it was taken so both runs started alike.

prompt: A table of sensor readings gets a new row every millisecond and is never updated. Which of these indexes adds the least write-ahead log per insert after each checkpoint?
hint: Where in the index does each new key land?

choices.text: An index on the sensor's id, with 50,000 sensors reporting in random order
choices.why: Random keys touch a different leaf page almost every time, and each page costs a full image once per checkpoint.

choices.text: An index on the reading's value, which jumps about
choices.why: Values that jump about land all over the index, like the lesson's `total_cents`.

choices.text: An index on the reading's timestamp
choices.why: Right: a value that only grows is added at the right-hand end, so the same few pages take every new key.

choices.text: All three add the same amount, since each insert adds one entry to each
choices.why: One entry each, but not one page image each: the page images depend on how many different pages the keys touch.

prompt: Which column says how many times queries have read an index since the counters were reset?
hint: It is in pg_stat_user_indexes.

choices.text: `pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_tup_read`, the entries returned
choices.why: That counts index entries returned, not how many scans started; the lesson reads the number of scans.

choices.text: `pg_index.indisvalid`
choices.why: That says whether an index can be used at all, for example after a failed concurrent build.

choices.text: `pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan`
choices.why: Right: one count per scan a query started on the index.

choices.text: `pg_stat_statements.calls`
choices.why: That counts executions of a statement, with no index named anywhere.

prompt: After the one-minute mix, `orders_customer_id_idx` showed 0 scans and `orders_customer_idx` 72,686. What does that zero mean?
hint: The two indexes have the same column.

choices.text: That the planner chose one of two identical indexes, and either could go
choices.why: Right: the zero records a tie the planner broke; once one twin goes, its scans move to the other.

choices.text: That the customer search is written to read only the newest index on `customer_id`
choices.why: The planner has no rule favouring newer indexes; it saw two equal choices.

choices.text: That `orders_customer_id_idx` is damaged in some way and should be rebuilt before anything else
choices.why: A damaged index is not what a zero means; the twin simply took the reads.

choices.text: That the original must be dropped and the newer one kept
choices.why: The counter cannot tell you which twin to keep; section 04 keeps the original for its name.

prompt: An index shows `idx_scan = 0` on the primary. Which of these could still mean it is needed? Choose all that apply.
hint: The four ways a zero lies.

choices.text: The counters were reset two days ago and a report runs monthly
choices.why: Right: the window is shorter than the cycle that reads it.

choices.text: Reports run against a read replica
choices.why: Right: the counters are per server, and the drop would reach the replica too.

choices.text: It backs a unique constraint
choices.why: Right: enforcing a rule leaves no trace in idx_scan.

choices.text: Its table has more than a million rows
choices.why: The size of the table says nothing about whether anybody reads the index.

choices.text: Its last_idx_scan is empty
choices.why: An empty last_idx_scan agrees with the zero; it is not a reason to keep the index.

prompt: `sellers_pkey` was scanned 29,010 times during the mix, although no workload script looks up a seller by id. What did the scanning?
hint: Every order names a seller.

choices.text: Autovacuum, which scans every primary key after a batch of inserts
choices.why: Autovacuum's work does not appear as idx_scan on another table's key.

choices.text: The seller dashboard's join
choices.why: The dashboard reads `orders` by `seller_id` and joins nothing; it used `orders_seller_placed_idx`.

choices.text: pg_stat_statements, while normalising queries
choices.why: The extension reads no tables to count statements.

choices.text: The foreign-key check run for each inserted order
choices.why: Right: each order proves its seller exists, and that proof is an index scan; customers_pkey shows the same 29,010.

prompt: You are asked to remove indexes on a server whose `stats_reset` is yesterday. A colleague reset the counters to measure a test. What do you do first?
hint: A zero needs a window.

choices.text: Drop every index the unused query lists, since a day of traffic is a fair sample
choices.why: A day misses the weekly, monthly and yearly jobs, exactly the lesson's monthly report.

choices.text: Wait until the counters cover the longest cycle the application has, or ask who runs the reports
choices.why: Right: the counter is only evidence over a window long enough for every job to have run.

choices.text: Restart the server so the counters are rebuilt from the log
choices.why: Counters are not rebuilt from the log; a clean restart keeps them, and nothing restores what the reset cleared.

choices.text: Read `last_idx_scan`, which survives a reset
choices.why: `last_idx_scan` is cleared by the same reset; it is useful only over a window the counters cover.

prompt: Why does `order_lines_product_id_idx1` end in `1`?
hint: Look at its line in leftovers.sql.

choices.text: It is the first version of the index, and the next migration to change it makes a 2
choices.why: PostgreSQL keeps no versions of an index in its name.

choices.text: It was built with one column, and PostgreSQL appends the column count to every name
choices.why: The suffix does not count columns; the original has one column too.

choices.text: It lives in tablespace 1
choices.why: The name says nothing about where the file lives.

choices.text: The migration gave no name, and PostgreSQL's own choice was already taken
choices.why: Right: `CREATE INDEX ON order_lines (product_id)` makes up a name, and adds 1 because `order_lines_product_id_idx` existed.

prompt: Two B-tree indexes on `products (title)`: one plain, one with `text_pattern_ops`. Why does the duplicate query not list them together?
hint: One of the five columns differs.

choices.text: Their `indclass` differs, so they store entries ordered for different questions
choices.why: Right: the operator class decides what the index can answer, so they are not the same index.

choices.text: Their names differ
choices.why: The query ignores names on purpose; the lesson's duplicates had different names.

choices.text: Text columns are skipped by the query, because their collations cannot be compared as text
choices.why: Nothing in the query filters by type; it compares the five columns of pg_index.

choices.text: One was built concurrently
choices.why: How an index was built is not recorded in what the query compares.

prompt: A table has a primary key on `id` and a plain index on `id` that the planner reads all day, while the primary key shows 0 scans. Which one do you drop?
hint: Which one can the server drop on its own?

choices.text: The primary key's index, because nobody reads it
choices.why: The server refuses to drop an index a constraint owns, and the constraint is the rule against a second row with the same id.

choices.text: The plain index; its reads move to the primary key
choices.why: Right: the zero was a tie the planner broke, and dropping the non-unique twin of a primary key is always safe.

choices.text: Neither, since the counts prove both are needed
choices.why: One of them has zero reads and the other has all of them; the counts prove one is spare.

choices.text: Both, and create a fresh unique index
choices.why: Dropping the primary key's index means dropping the key, and rebuilding costs time for nothing.

prompt: The duplicate query groups `pg_index` by `indkey`, `indclass`, `indcollation`, `indexprs` and `___`, the WHERE of a partial index.
hint: The column whose name starts with ind and ends with the word for a condition.

prompt: Why can an index on `(seller_id, placed_at)` answer `WHERE seller_id = 42` without any help?
hint: How is the index sorted?

choices.text: Because the planner rewrites the query to add a range on `placed_at`
choices.why: No rewrite happens; the plan's Index Cond is just `seller_id = 42`.

choices.text: It is sorted by `seller_id` first
choices.why: Right: all of seller 42's entries sit together, so reading the first column is enough.

choices.text: Because B-trees can be read from either column
choices.why: A B-tree on (a, b) is not sorted by b on its own; only the leading column works this way.

choices.text: Because `placed_at` is never null
choices.why: Nulls are not the reason; the order of the columns is.

prompt: Of the pair `orders_placed_at_idx` and `orders_placed_at_status_idx`, the lesson drops the longer one, against the usual rule. Why?
hint: What did the monthly report read?

choices.text: Because two-column indexes cannot be read for a range
choices.why: They can; a range on the first column works on (placed_at, status) too.

choices.text: Because `status` changes in every order, so the composite costs every update its HOT as well
choices.why: `place-order.sql` never updates `status`; that was the reason for `total_cents`, not here.

choices.text: Nothing read the composite, even the report built for it, and it is the bigger one
choices.why: Right: the report read the single-column index, and the composite was 79 MB against 44.

choices.text: Because indexes created by `market.sql` can never be dropped, so the shorter one has to stay
choices.why: Any index a constraint does not own can be dropped; the lesson dropped `orders_seller_id_idx`, added in lesson 2.

prompt: `customers` has a unique index on `(email)` and a plain index on `(email, city)`. The overlapping query lists the pair with `shorter_is_unique = t`. What is safe?
hint: What does each index forbid?

choices.text: Dropping `(email)`, since the longer one covers it
choices.why: The longer index allows two rows with the same email; dropping the unique one drops the rule.

choices.text: Dropping both and adding a unique index on `(email, city)`
choices.why: Unique on the pair allows the same email in two cities; that is a weaker rule.

choices.text: Nothing can be decided without the table's size
choices.why: The size matters for the hot-lookup case, but uniqueness settles which one must stay.

choices.text: Keeping `(email)`; the longer one goes if its reads move
choices.why: Right: the unique index enforces a rule, so if one goes it is the longer, after its reads are checked.

prompt: Match each leftover to what the lesson decided about it.
hint: Sections 03 to 05.

pairs.right: dropped: overlapped by a longer index that is read
dropped: unread, and it cost every update its HOT
dropped: an exact copy of an older index
kept: the operations screen reads it

prompt: What does `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` answer inside `BEGIN … COMMIT`?
hint: The lesson ran it once that way.

choices.text: It waits for the COMMIT and then drops the index
choices.why: It does not wait; it refuses at once.

choices.text: It drops the index without the concurrency
choices.why: It does not fall back to a plain drop; it raises an error.

choices.text: An error: it cannot run inside a transaction block
choices.why: Right: it commits more than once on its own, so it refuses an outer transaction.

choices.text: A warning, and the drop is rolled back with the rest
choices.why: It is an error, and the transaction is left failed, which is why the transcript shows `market=!#`.

prompt: Why save the output of `pg_get_indexdef` before dropping, when PostgreSQL 16 has no way to disable an index?
hint: What is the only way back after a drop?

choices.text: Because the server needs it to drop the index concurrently
choices.why: The drop needs only the name; the definition is for you.

choices.text: Because rebuilding is the only way back, and it should be the exact statement, reviewed
choices.why: Right: with no switch to turn an index off, the undo is a build from the stored definition, in the migration's reverse step.

choices.text: Because `DROP INDEX` also deletes the index's definition from the migration files that created it
choices.why: The server never touches your migration files.

choices.text: Because the statistics of the index are lost otherwise
choices.why: pg_get_indexdef returns a CREATE INDEX statement, not statistics.

prompt: After the six drops, how many bytes of write-ahead log did each order write, according to the lesson's last measurement?
hint: The table at the end of the section.

prompt: Put the steps of dropping an index you think is unused in the order the lesson takes them.
hint: The way back comes before the drop.
items: Check idx_scan over a window covering every cycle, on every server
Run DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY outside a transaction block
Measure the workload again and compare
trap: Saving the definition after the drop is too late: it reads the catalogue, and the index is no longer in it.

prompt: A busy `payments` table has an unread index on `status`, and every payment is updated from `pending` to `paid`. A teammate wants to drop it with plain `DROP INDEX` at noon. What two things does the lesson say about that plan?
hint: One about the payoff, one about the method.

choices.text: The payoff is tiny because the index is small, and plain DROP is fine at noon
choices.why: An index on an updated column costs HOT on every update, whatever its size, and a plain drop queues every query behind its lock.

choices.text: Dropping it brings HOT back to every update, and it should be dropped concurrently
choices.why: Right: `status` changes in each update, so the index blocks HOT; and a plain drop waits for, then blocks, the busy table.

choices.text: It must first be rebuilt, then dropped
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson rebuilds an index before dropping it.

choices.text: Unread indexes on status columns are always kept for the planner's statistics
choices.why: The planner's statistics come from ANALYZE on the table, not from indexes on plain columns.
